sections.h: Romans 1–4: the world's guilt and God's righteousness
sections.b: The first four chapters set out the problem and the answer. Paul greets a church he has not visited (1:1–15), states his theme, that the good news is God's power for everyone who believes because God's righteousness is revealed in it (1:16–17), and then shows that Gentiles (1:18–32), Jewish teachers (2:1–29) and Israel itself (3:1–20) are all under sin. At 3:21 God's righteousness is made plain in Christ, whom God put forward as the place of atonement, and chapter 4 proves from Abraham that this righteousness has always come by faith.

common: Churches that teach justification by faith (and others, in different language) draw on Romans 1–4.
uncommon: Some scholars read the first four chapters mainly as a plea for Jewish and Gentile believers to accept each other (Stowers, Wright), with the doctrine of the individual's justification as a part of that.

sections.h: Paul writes to a church he had not met (Romans 1–4)
sections.b: Romans is the longest of Paul's letters and the only undisputed one addressed to a church he neither founded nor yet visited. In it he calls himself a slave of Christ Jesus, called as an apostle and set apart for the good news of God (1:1), whose task is to bring about "the obedience of faith" among all the Gentiles (1:5). He writes in the winter of about AD 56–57 from Corinth, with a scribe named Tertius (16:22), before taking the collection to Jerusalem. He argues as a Jew: from the Scriptures, from Abraham, and in the style of a Jewish teacher's lecture with an imagined partner.

Paul's answer to "How can a person be right with God?" is given in the central paragraph of the letter. All have sinned (3:23), and are justified freely, by God's grace, through the redemption in Christ Jesus (3:24), received by faith, apart from works of the law (3:28). God does this in a way that shows he is righteous himself (3:26). Abraham is the proof: his faith was reckoned as righteousness before he was circumcised (4:3, 9–10), and God is the One who justifies the ungodly (4:5). The phrase "works of the law" (3:20, 28) is read by Reformation interpreters as any deeds done to earn favor and by the New Perspective as the law's badges of Jewish identity.

sections.h: Judgment by works and justification by faith
sections.b: Paul says that God "will pay back each person according to his works" (2:6) and that the doers of the law "will be justified" (2:13), and also that no one is justified by works of the law (3:20). The churches reconcile the two differently: as a standard no one meets without grace (Luther), as the fruit of faith that will be judged (Reformed, Lutheran), as works done by grace that merit eternal life (Catholic), or as the life the Spirit produces (Cranfield, Wright).

common: Paul teaches that justification is God's free gift, received by faith, not earned by works of the law.
uncommon: Paul's "faith of Jesus Christ" (3:22, 26) may mean Christ's own faithfulness and not our faith in him (Hays, Campbell).

sections.b: Romans begins and ends its argument about faith with Scripture: "The righteous will live by faith" (Habakkuk 2:4, quoted at Romans 1:17) and "Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6, quoted at Romans 4:3). Faith here is trust in the God who gives life to the dead (4:17–21) and who raised Jesus (4:24). The Greek pistis also means faithfulness, and Paul uses it of God in 3:3. The phrase "faith of Jesus Christ" (3:22, 26) can mean faith in Christ or Christ's faithfulness; the Plain follows the first and notes the second.
sections.refs: Habakkuk 2:4; Genesis 15:6; Romans 1:17; Romans 3:3; Romans 3:22; Romans 4:3; Romans 4:17–24; James 2:21–24

sections.b: Paul greets the Romans with "grace to you and peace" (1:7) and says he received grace and the work of an apostle (1:5). In 3:24 sinners are justified "freely, by his grace." In 4:4–6 grace is set against wages: what is earned is a debt, but what is given is a favor, and faith is reckoned as righteousness. In 4:16 the promise depends on faith "so that it will be by grace" and certain for all of Abraham's offspring. John Barclay argues that for Paul grace is unconditioned, though not without demand.

Paul says that God's anger "is revealed from heaven" against people who hold the truth down (1:18), at the same time as his righteousness is revealed in the good news (1:17). The anger is shown now in God's handing humanity over to what it chose (1:24, 26, 28) and will be shown on "the day of anger" (2:5). It falls on all who do evil, "for the Jew first and for the Greek as well" (2:9). C. H. Dodd read it as an impersonal moral process; Cranfield, Morris and Stott as God's personal and steady opposition to evil. The Plain writes "anger" for orge.

Romans has the Bible's fullest statement of the idea. God's "invisible qualities, his everlasting power and divine nature" are visible to the mind in what he has made, so that people who ignore him have no defense (1:19–20). Gentiles who do what the law contains by nature show the work of the law written on their hearts, and their conscience bears witness (2:14–15). The churches differ over what this knowledge can do: lead people to God (Catholic), leave them without excuse but not save (Reformed, Lutheran, Baptist), or nothing at all (Barth).
sections.refs: Romans 1:19–20; Romans 2:14–15; Psalm 19:1–4; Acts 14:15–17; Acts 17:22–31; Wisdom of Solomon 13:1–9

sections.b: Romans 3:25 is the one place where Paul calls Christ the hilasterion, the "place of atonement," the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the lid of the ark, where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). "By his blood" ties the death to sacrifice. The same verse speaks of God's forbearance in passing over earlier sins and of the showing of his righteousness (3:25–26). Whether the word means propitiation (turning aside God's anger), expiation (removing sin) or the atonement lid is debated. In 4:25 Jesus is "handed over for our trespasses," in the words of Isaiah 53:12.
sections.refs: Romans 3:24–26; Romans 4:25; Leviticus 16:2; Leviticus 16:14–15; Leviticus 17:11; Exodus 25:17–22; Isaiah 53:12; Hebrews 9:5

sections.b: Romans 1:18–3:20 is the Bible's longest argument that all humanity is sinful. Paul says Jews and Greeks alike are "under sin" (3:9), supports it with a chain of Psalms and Isaiah (3:10–18), and concludes that all sinned and lack God's glory (3:23). Here sin is a power that rules people, not only a list of acts. The law does not free anyone from it; it gives knowledge of sin (3:20) and makes sin visible as transgression (4:15).

Paul's thesis is that the good news "is God's power for salvation for everyone who believes, first for the Jew and for the Greek as well." In Romans salvation is mostly future: rescue from the coming anger on the day of judgment (5:9–10; 13:11), begun now by justification and reconciliation. The question whether those who never heard the gospel can be saved runs through 2:12–16; the churches answer it differently.

Romans 1:26–27 is the longest New Testament passage on the question. Paul says God handed humanity over to shameful passions: women "changed the natural use for one that goes against nature," and men "gave up the natural use of the woman and burned in their desire for one another." The passage is part of an argument about idolatry (1:18–32), and it leads to 2:1, where the reader who judges is told to look at himself. Readers differ on what "nature" means, whether the passage speaks of all same-sex acts or of excess, and what role it plays in Paul's argument. The churches' positions are on the card at 1:26–27.

common: Paul's words belong to the Jewish condemnation of Gentile idolatry and its consequences; they are not a systematic treatise on sexual ethics.
uncommon: The passage may be a rhetorical setup for 2:1 and not a statement of Paul's own ethic (Stowers).

sections.b: Paul traces idolatry to a refusal: people knew God but did not praise him or give thanks, and so they "traded the glory of the immortal God for a likeness" of humans and animals (1:21–23). The Greek echoes Psalm 106:20, where Israel "traded their glory for the shape of an ox," and Jeremiah 2:11. Paul calls the result "the lie" (1:25) and says God handed the idolaters over to their desires. The sequence from idols to moral disorder follows the Wisdom of Solomon (13–14), a book that is Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians.
sections.refs: Romans 1:21–25; Psalm 106:20; Jeremiah 2:11; Wisdom of Solomon 13:1–14:31

sections.h: The Jew first, and the Jew's advantage (Romans 1–4)
sections.b: In the first four chapters Paul says the good news is for "first for the Jew and for the Greek as well" (1:16), that Jews also face judgment by deeds (2:9), that a real Jew is one whose circumcision is of the heart (2:28–29), that the Jew has "much" advantage because Israel was put in charge of the oracles of God (3:1–2), and that Abraham is father of both the circumcised who share his faith and the uncircumcised who believe (4:11–12, 16). Chapters 9–11, written by another part, return to the question. Readers differ on whether 2:28–29 takes the name "Jew" from Israel or calls Israel to its own calling.

Paul says circumcision "is of value" if one keeps the law, but is worthless for a lawbreaker (2:25), that a person is a real Jew by circumcision of the heart (2:28–29), and that Abraham received it as a sign and seal of a righteousness he already had by faith, so that he is father of the uncircumcised who believe and of the circumcised who walk in his steps (4:9–12). The prophets had already said that the heart must be circumcised (Deuteronomy 10:16; 30:6; Jeremiah 4:4).
sections.refs: Romans 2:25–29; Romans 4:9–12; Genesis 17:10–14; Deuteronomy 10:16; Deuteronomy 30:6; Jeremiah 4:4; Jeremiah 9:25–26

sections.b: Paul calls Abraham "our forefather according to the flesh" (4:1) and uses Genesis 15:6 to show that he was reckoned righteous by faith, before he was circumcised (4:3–12). He is father of all who believe, Jew and Gentile (4:11–12, 16–17), heir of the world (4:13), and the model of trust in the God who gives life to the dead (4:17–21). The Jewish tradition of Abraham as the faithful and tested servant (Sirach 44 and 1 Maccabees 2:52, Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians; Jubilees 23, Scripture only for the Ethiopian Orthodox church) is the background Paul answers; James 2:21–24 reads the same verse differently.
sections.refs: Romans 4:1–25; Genesis 15:1–6; Genesis 17:1–27; Sirach 44:19–21; 1 Maccabees 2:52; James 2:21–24; Galatians 3:6–18

sections.b: Paul takes the law seriously and says it has limits. Hearers are not righteous, but doers will be justified (2:13); Gentiles show "the work of the law" written on their hearts (2:15); the law gives knowledge of sin (3:20) and produces anger (4:15); and faith does not cancel the law but makes it stand (3:31). "Works of the law" (3:20, 28) is read as any deeds the law requires or as the law's badges of Jewish identity. Christians differ on whether the law remains binding in any part (see the topic page).

Romans is addressed "to all God's loved ones in Rome" (1:7). The church was not founded by an apostle. It met in several house groups, drew Jews and Gentiles, and had been shaken by the edict of Claudius (about AD 49), which expelled Jews, among them Aquila and Priscilla (Acts 18:2; Suetonius, Claudius 25.4). Tacitus reports a vast multitude of Christians in Rome by AD 64 (Annals 15.44). Paul's "in Rome" is missing from a few manuscripts at 1:7 and 1:15.

sections.h: Christ as the place of atonement (Romans 3:25)
sections.b: Paul calls Christ the place of atonement "by his blood" (3:25), using the language of the Day of Atonement and of the temple's sacrifices. The Plain's "atonement lid" for the ark's cover (Exodus 25:17–22) is the same Greek word as the "place of atonement." The text does not say that the sacrifice of Leviticus is the same as the cross, but that Christ does what the lid and the blood stood for. Hebrews works the idea out at length.

The blood of Romans 3:25 recalls Leviticus 17:11: "a body's life is in its blood ... It is the blood that makes atonement, by means of the life in it." Paul's phrase can be read as the sacrifice of Jesus' death, as life offered to God, or as the means of cleansing; the Greek links it to faith in a way that can be read two ways. He speaks again of justification "by his blood" in 5:9.

Paul puts the resurrection at the beginning (1:4, Jesus "marked out as Son of God with power by his resurrection from the dead") and the end (4:24–25, "raised for our justification") of the first part of the letter. Abraham's faith is the faith in the God who "makes the dead alive" (4:17), and ours is faith in the One who raised Jesus (4:24). The Jewish Amidah's second blessing praises God who gives life to the dead.

Paul speaks of the "glory" of God that humanity swapped for images (1:23) and lacks (3:23). Several Jewish writings that are in no church's Bible speak of Adam's lost glory (1QS 4:23; Life of Adam and Eve). Later in the letter the glory is promised to those who are in Christ (5:2; 8:17–30), and Abraham is the one who "gave glory to God" (4:20). Whether 3:23 refers to Adam's glory is debated (Dunn, Moo).
sections.refs: Romans 1:23; Romans 3:23; Romans 4:20; Romans 5:2; Romans 8:17–30; Psalm 8:5

sections.b: Paul's phrase "Spirit of holiness" is a Hebrew-style way of saying the Holy Spirit (compare Psalm 51:11). By the Spirit Jesus is marked out as Son of God with power at the resurrection. In 2:29 circumcision is "of the heart, in spirit and not in letter," which may mean the human spirit or the Holy Spirit. The full teaching on the Spirit in Romans comes in chapters 5–8.

sections.h: The Son of God in power (Romans 1:3–4)
sections.b: Romans 1:3–4 is probably an early confession: the Son came from David's line according to the flesh and was marked out as Son of God with power by his resurrection. The word "marked out" (horizo) has raised the question whether Jesus became Son only then (adoptionism, which the church rejected); the usual reply is that he is already God's Son in 1:3 and 8:3, and the resurrection marks a new stage of authority.

Paul begins the letter by saying the Son "came from the offspring of David." It connects Jesus to the promise made to David (2 Samuel 7:12–16), and he returns to the idea in 15:12, where the root of Jesse rises to rule the nations.

Paul's word for his message, euangelion, was already used of announcements about the emperor. The calendar inscription of Priene (9 BC) calls the birthday of Augustus the beginning of the good news for the world. Paul fills the word with the content of Isaiah 52:7. Whether he meant an open contrast with Caesar's good news is debated; the opening of Romans, with its titles for Jesus (Son of God, Lord), would have sounded strong to Roman ears.

The Greek hilasterion of Romans 3:25 is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the atonement lid of the ark, the place where the high priest sprinkled blood on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:14–15; Hebrews 9:5). Luther rendered it "Gnadenstuhl," seat of grace. Paul's use of the word has been read as a reference to the day, to the lid, or to sacrifice in general.

To show that David also teaches justification without works, Paul quotes Psalm 32:1–2: the blessed are those "whose lawless acts have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered over," and the man whose sin the Lord will never reckon. He links the Psalm to Genesis 15:6 by the shared word "reckon."

Paul asks the person who judges whether he makes light of "the riches of his kindness, his forbearance and his patience," not realizing that God's kindness is meant to lead to repentance. The words echo Exodus 34:6. God's forbearance is also the reason he passed over earlier sins (3:25).

"With God there are no favorites" (2:11) takes up the teaching of Deuteronomy 10:17 and 2 Chronicles 19:7. Paul pairs it with the question whether God is just to bring anger on sinners whose sin shows his righteousness (3:5–6), and answers: God must be able to judge the world.

The oldest large copy of Romans is the papyrus P46 (about AD 200), but its surviving leaves begin at 5:17; for chapters 1–4 the oldest witnesses are fragments such as the third-century papyrus P40. In Romans 1–4 the main variants are the omission of "in Rome" at 1:7 and 1:15 in Codex Boernerianus, the words "of Christ" added at 1:16, "and upon all" at 3:22, the verb "found" at 4:1, and a "not" before "considered" at 4:19. Marcion's text of Romans, reported by Origen in Rufinus' Latin, is said to have left out the last chapters.
sections.refs: Romans 1:7; Romans 1:15; Romans 1:16; Romans 3:22; Romans 4:1; Romans 4:19

sections.b: Paul opens the letter by calling himself a slave (doulos) of Christ Jesus. The title, used of Moses, David and the prophets in the Greek Old Testament, claims both ownership by Christ and authority from him. In Rome it would have recalled the powerful slaves of the emperor's household. Paul develops the picture in 6:15–23.

sections.h: The law written on the heart (Romans 2:15, 29)
sections.b: Paul's words "written in their hearts" (2:15) and "circumcision ... of the heart, in spirit and not in letter" (2:29) use the language of the new covenant promised in Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 36:26–27 and of the heart circumcision of Deuteronomy 30:6. Whether he applies it to Gentile Christians only, or to the witness of every conscience, is debated.

Genesis promises Abraham's offspring a land (Genesis 12:7; 15:18). In Romans 4:13 Paul says the promise was that he would "inherit the world." The widening was already in Sirach 44:21 (Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians), where God promises that Abraham's offspring will inherit from sea to sea. For Paul the promise reaches the nations and the whole creation (4:16–17; 8:19–23).
sections.refs: Romans 4:13; Genesis 12:7; Genesis 15:18; Genesis 22:17–18; Sirach 44:21; Romans 8:19–23

sections.b: Paul uses the Jewish confession that God is one (Deuteronomy 6:4) to argue that he is God of Gentiles as well as Jews and will justify both by the same faith (3:29–30). The argument is made from within Jewish belief about God.

Paul calls Jesus "our Lord" at the end of the first long sentence (1:4). The Greek Old Testament uses "Lord" (Kyrios) for God's name; in 10:9 and 10:13 Paul applies that name to Jesus. This site writes "the Lord" (never "the LORD") for Kyrios in the New Testament.

sections.h: Serving God in the good news (Romans 1:9)
sections.b: Paul says he serves God "with my spirit in the good news of his Son." The verb latreuo is the Greek Bible's word for worship and service in the tabernacle and temple. Paul thinks of preaching as a form of worship (1:9; 15:16) and of the whole life as a sacrifice (12:1).

Paul wants to share "some spiritual gift" with the Romans to make them strong (1:11), and immediately adds that he will be encouraged by them (1:12). He does not say what the gift is. Gifts are listed in 12:6–8.

Paul tests the Jewish teacher with the commandments: "You announce, 'Do not steal.' Do you steal? You say, 'Do not commit adultery.' Do you commit adultery?" The commandments are from Exodus 20:14–15 and Deuteronomy 5:17–19.

Paul says the Jews were put in charge of "the oracles of God" (3:2). The Greek logia means God's sayings; it can refer to the Scriptures as a whole or to the promises within them. Acts 7:38 calls the law received at Sinai "living oracles."
